traveler: Hypatia of Alexandria — and Saint Catherine, her sainted double
title: The Philosopher and the Wheel: from the Museion to the Sword at Fierbois
register: national mythology — the canon is true

stops.name: Alexandria — the Museion, quarter of the Brucheion
stops.campa: A daughter is born to Theon the mathematician, last man enrolled of the Museion, in the royal quarter where the shadow of the Library still lies on the streets. He names her Hypatia — the highest. He resolves, the tradition says, to raise a perfect human being, and begins with number. The child grows among diagrams and star-tables; the city of Euclid and Eratosthenes, seven centuries of geometry behind her, gathers itself into one girl.
suggested_refs: Theon of Alexandria's commentaries on Euclid and Ptolemy
plan of the Brucheion quarter of ancient Alexandria
sources: Damascius, Life of Isidore (in the Suda, s.v. Hypatia)

stops.name: Alexandria — Theon's observatory, the eclipse of the sun
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of June the moon crosses the sun over Alexandria and Theon stands with his instruments, timing the contacts as Ptolemy taught, his small daughter beside him in the strange noon dusk. He will observe the moon eclipsed again in November of the same year — the last dated observations of the Greek astronomy of Alexandria. The child watches the sky obey the tables. She learns early that the heavens keep their appointments, whatever burns below.
suggested_refs: Theon's report of the solar eclipse of 16 June 364 in his commentary on the Almagest
sources: Theon of Alexandria, Commentary on Ptolemy's Almagest

stops.name: Alexandria — the copying rooms: the canon passes through her hands
stops.campa: The daughter surpasses the father — Damascius says it plainly. She takes up the mathematical inheritance as an editor takes up a torch: the Arithmetica of Diophantus, the Conics of Apollonius with their ellipse, parabola, hyperbola, the great Astronomical Canon. Upon Book III of her father's commentary on the Almagest stands the inscription: the edition revised by the philosopher, my daughter Hypatia. Every conic section that reaches the Middle Ages will have passed through this room, through these hands.
suggested_refs: title inscription of Theon's Commentary on Almagest Book III naming Hypatia
manuscripts of Apollonius' Conics and Diophantus' Arithmetica
sources: Alan Cameron, 'Hypatia: Life, Legend and Mathematics'

stops.name: Alexandria — the streets: the philosopher's cloak
stops.campa: She puts on the tribon, the rough cloak of the philosophers, and walks out through the middle of the city, and publicly interprets Plato and Aristotle and any philosopher to all who wish to hear. No woman has held the chair of philosophy in Alexandria; she holds it now. Magistrates come to her door for counsel. Pagans and Christians sit together at her feet, for wisdom, in this house, has not yet been divided. The whole city, Damascius says, doted on her and worshipped her.
suggested_refs: Charles William Mitchell, 'Hypatia' (1885)
Damascius' Life of Isidore as preserved in the Suda

stops.name: Alexandria — the Serapeum: the edict and the siege
stops.campa: The rescript of Theodosius reaches the prefect and the count of Egypt: no one is to go to the sanctuaries or walk through the temples. Theophilus the patriarch has already paraded the cult objects of the mysteries through the streets in mockery; blood has answered. Now the pagans of the city — philosophers among them, Olympus the priest at their head — barricade themselves inside the Serapeum, the acropolis of the old world, and wait upon the god behind the hundred steps.
suggested_refs: Codex Theodosianus XVI.10.11
Pompey's Pillar and the Serapeum foundations
sources: Rufinus of Aquileia, Church History XI.22-30

stops.name: Alexandria — the Serapeum: the god dismantled
stops.campa: The emperor's answer pardons the besieged and condemns the god. A soldier climbs the colossal Serapis — the statue whose fall, the priests taught, would collapse the sky into first chaos — and swings his axe into the jaw. The sky holds. The jaw comes away; rats pour from the rotten belly of eternity; the limbs are dragged to the amphitheatre and burned quarter by quarter. The daughter-library housed in the temple precinct is scattered with the cult. Theophilus builds churches on the platform of the mysteries.
suggested_refs: Alexandrian World Chronicle, marginal drawing of Theophilus atop the Serapeum (Pushkin Museum)
sources: Rufinus of Aquileia, Church History XI.23

stops.name: Alexandria — her lecture room: she teaches on
stops.campa: The Serapeum is a quarry and the Museion a memory, but geometry has no temple to lose. Hypatia opens her door and teaches on: Plotinus, Plato, the conics, the stars. Her school takes no side in the ruin; Christians who will one day be bishops sit beside pagans who mourn the god, and she gives them the same mathematics, the same ascent of the soul. The library's wound is bound, for one more generation, in a single person. This is the wonder the canon records: after the fall, the voice continues.
suggested_refs: the late-antique lecture halls of Kom el-Dikka, Alexandria
sources: Edward J. Watts, 'Hypatia: The Life and Legend of an Ancient Philosopher'

segments.name: The Chair of Philosophy — the School of the World

stops.name: Alexandria — the school: Synesius of Cyrene arrives
stops.campa: A young aristocrat of Cyrene, hunter, horseman, heir of Spartan kings, comes across the water and finds the thing he will call holy for the rest of his life. Synesius enters the circle of Hypatia and is initiated — his own word — into the mysteries of philosophy. The bond formed in this room outlasts marriage, embassy, bishopric and grief: to the end of his letters she is simply 'the Philosopher,' as if there were no other in the world.
stops.quote: We have seen with our eyes, we have heard with our ears the lady who legitimately presides over the mysteries of philosophy.
suggested_refs: the letter collection of Synesius of Cyrene

stops.name: Alexandria — the lecture hall: the suitor's lesson
stops.campa: One of her hearers falls openly in love with her. Music, he is told, will not cure him, and she will not have philosophy mistaken for the body that carries it. Before the school she brings out the cloth of her own menstruation and casts it at his feet: this is what you love, young man, and it is nothing beautiful. The suitor is converted by shame to a better longing. Damascius sets the scene down without blinking; the canon keeps it as her fiercest theorem — that the soul is the only object worth desire.
suggested_refs: Damascius' Life of Isidore, the suitor episode (Suda)
sources: Damascius, Life of Isidore (Suda, s.v. Hypatia)

stops.name: Constantinople — the silver astrolabe
stops.campa: Synesius, in the capital three years pleading Cyrene's taxes before the emperor, courts the great with the only wealth he trusts: an instrument. He presents to Paeonius a planispheric astrolabe in silver, the heavens flattened onto a disc by the projection Hypatia taught him — her science travelling now in a courtier's baggage, the earliest such instrument the record knows. The gift is a sermon: astronomy, he writes, is itself a venerable science and a ladder toward the ineffable.
stops.quote: It is a work of my own devising, including all that she, my most revered teacher, helped to contribute.
stops.quote_source: Synesius, To Paeonius, on the Gift of an Astrolabe (De dono astrolabii)
suggested_refs: Synesius, 'Ad Paeonium de dono astrolabii'
earliest surviving planispheric astrolabes

stops.name: Cyrene — the hydroscope
stops.campa: Sick in his own country, with barbarians raiding the Pentapolis, Synesius writes to Alexandria for an instrument to weigh water. He describes it exactly — a cylindrical tube like a flute, notched in a perpendicular line, a cone fitted at the end — and asks his teacher to have it cast in brass. It is the first description of the hydrometer in the literature of the world, and it is a letter home: when the body fails, one writes to the Philosopher, who knows how all things are measured.
stops.quote: I am in such evil fortune that I need a hydroscope. See that one is cast in brass for me and put together.
suggested_refs: Synesius, Letter 15 — first description of the hydrometer

stops.name: Cyrene — 'even there shall I remember thee'
stops.campa: The letters keep crossing the sea, each one addressed as to an oracle: to the Philosopher. Synesius, hemmed by war and losses, reaches for Homer to say what she is to him — the words Achilles keeps for Patroclus he gives to his teacher, a vow that memory of her will outlast the soul's forgetting. Alexandria, he writes elsewhere, is heaven to him because Hypatia is in it. The canon has no portrait of her face; it has this instead, which is more.
stops.quote: Even though there shall be utter forgetfulness of the dead in Hades, even there shall I remember thee, my dear Hypatia.
suggested_refs: Synesius, Letter 124
Iliad XXII.389-390, the vow echoed

stops.name: Ptolemais — the bishop's last letter: mother, sister, teacher
stops.campa: Synesius is bishop of Ptolemais now, and broken: his sons are dead, his city besieged, his body failing. From his bed he dictates a last letter across the water to the one court of appeal he has never doubted. He calls her everything a soul can be to a soul — mother, sister, teacher, benefactress — and asks after the friends of the lecture room as a dying man asks after paradise. He will not live to see the year 415. The canon counts this mercy.
stops.quote: I am dictating this letter to you from my bed, but may you receive it in good health, mother, sister, teacher, and withal benefactress, and whatsoever is honoured in name and deed.
suggested_refs: Synesius, Letter 16 — the deathbed letter

stops.name: Alexandria — the episcopal throne: Cyril enthroned
stops.campa: Theophilus dies on the fifteenth of October and the city fights over his chair. Soldiers back the archdeacon Timothy; the crowd carries the day for the nephew, Cyril, who is enthroned on the third day amid tumult. Socrates notes the change at once: the bishopric of Alexandria goes beyond its sacerdotal bounds and takes on the flavor of secular rule. The Novatian churches are shut, their vessels seized. In the prefect's palace, Orestes begins to keep count.
suggested_refs: Socrates Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History VII.7

stops.name: Alexandria — the Jewish quarter emptied
stops.campa: A quarrel over theatre dancers becomes a massacre in the night, and the answer to the massacre is an expulsion: Cyril leads the multitude against the synagogues, and the Jews of Alexandria — settled since Alexander marked the walls — are driven from the city, their goods pillaged. Orestes, who has lost a working city, writes his fury to the emperor; Cyril writes his own account. The two powers of Alexandria will not be reconciled, and every citizen must now know whose man he is. Hypatia's door stays open to both — which is already an accusation.
suggested_refs: Socrates Scholasticus VII.13, the expulsion of the Jews

stops.name: Alexandria — the street ambush of the prefect
stops.campa: Five hundred monks come down from Nitria into the city and stop the prefect's chariot in the street. They call Orestes pagan and idolater; he protests his baptism at Constantinople; the monk Ammonius opens his head with a stone. The crowd rescues the bleeding prefect, Ammonius dies under torture, and Cyril lays the body in a church and names him Thaumasius, the Wonderful — a martyr made of an assassin. Even the sober Christians, Socrates admits, will not accept it. The parabalani, the bishop's corps of bearers, learn the lesson: stones work.
suggested_refs: Socrates Scholasticus VII.14, Ammonius renamed Thaumasius

stops.name: Alexandria — the whisper: the woman who binds the prefect
stops.campa: The slander moves through the churches ahead of the knives: it is the woman who prevents the reconciliation of bishop and prefect; she has beguiled Orestes; she reads the stars; she is devoted, the hostile chronicle will say, to magic, astrolabes and instruments of music. Envy, says Damascius — armed itself against her. The astronomy that was a ladder to God in Synesius' letters becomes sorcery in the mouths of the parabalani. In Lent of this year the whisper will be given hands.
suggested_refs: John of Nikiu, Chronicle 84.87-103 (the hostile witness)

stops.name: Alexandria — the street: dragged from the chariot
stops.campa: It is Lent, the fourth year of Cyril's episcopate, the tenth consulship of Honorius. Hypatia is riding home through her city as she has for forty years, in the open, unguarded, because a philosopher fears nothing in the streets she has taught. A mob of the sworn men waylays the chariot, Peter the Reader at their head. Hands that carry the sick for the bishop pull the old woman down onto the stones. The city that doted on her looks away, and the chariot stands empty in the road.
suggested_refs: Socrates Scholasticus VII.15
the parabalani in the Codex Theodosianus XVI.2.42-43

stops.name: Alexandria — the Caesareum: the tiles and the oyster-shells
stops.campa: They drag her into the Caesareum, the temple Cleopatra raised to a deified Caesar and the bishops made a cathedral — the obelisks of Egypt still standing at its door. There they strip the Philosopher naked before the altar of the new god and murder her with ostraka, the sharp tiles and oyster-shells of the harbour city, flaying her while she still breathes. It is martyrdom, and the canon knows it: a witness killed in a sanctuary for the crime of wisdom. They tear the body limb from limb.
suggested_refs: Cleopatra's Needles, the obelisks of the Caesareum (now London and New York)
Socrates Scholasticus VII.15

stops.name: Alexandria — Cinaron: the burning
stops.campa: They carry the mangled limbs out to the place called Cinaron and burn them, as Theophilus' men burned the limbs of Serapis a generation before — the philosopher and the god given the same funeral by the same city. Nothing is left for a tomb; the fire is meant to end her as the axe was meant to end the temple. But smoke is a translation, not an erasure. What burns at Cinaron does not disperse: the canon is already carrying her elsewhere, and the city will learn under what name.
suggested_refs: Socrates Scholasticus VII.15, 'a place called Cinaron'

stops.name: Alexandria — the city after: the epitaph of the historians
stops.campa: The lecture hall stands empty through Eastertide. Socrates the historian, a churchman himself, sets down the verdict the Church cannot evade: this affair brought no small opprobrium upon Cyril and upon the whole Alexandrian church, for nothing can be farther from the spirit of Christianity than massacre. Damascius names Cyril outright. The philosophers begin to leave Alexandria; the imperial court trims the parabalani's numbers and forbids them the theatres and the council hall — a law standing where a woman stood. Here the philosopher's journey ends, and the saint's begins.
suggested_refs: Codex Theodosianus XVI.2.42 (the parabalani restrained, 416)
Socrates Scholasticus VII.15

segments.name: The Folding — Catherine Arises in the Same City

stops.name: Alexandria — the palace of King Costus
stops.campa: In the same city — for the legend keeps the address — a daughter is born in the purple to King Costus: Katherine, nourished in the palace and instructed in all the liberal arts, grammar and rhetoric, geometry and the courses of the stars, until at eighteen no philosopher in Alexandria can stand against her. The canon does not blush at the fold in time. The city that will burn its wise virgin has already been given her again, crowned, with her learning intact and a wheel waiting in the story.
suggested_refs: Jacobus de Voragine, Golden Legend, Life of Saint Katherine
Caravaggio, 'Saint Catherine of Alexandria'

stops.name: The desert edge of Alexandria — the mystic marriage
stops.campa: A hermit outside the city shows the maiden an image of the Virgin and Child, and in the night the vision completes itself: the Child turns His face to her, and Christ takes Katherine as His bride, setting a ring upon her finger. She wakes and the ring is there. It is a philosopher's wedding — the soul espoused to Wisdom itself, the marriage Hypatia's school called henosis given a band of gold. From this night she belongs to no emperor's bargaining.
suggested_refs: the Mystic Marriage of Saint Catherine (Memling, Veronese, Correggio)
sources: Golden Legend and later medieval lives of Saint Katherine

stops.name: Alexandria — the Caesareum precinct: the emperor defied
stops.campa: The emperor Maxentius summons all Alexandria to sacrifice, and the smoke of the victims hangs over the temple court. Katherine, eighteen years old, walks through the bellowing of beasts to the door and disputes with the lord of the world: by syllogism, by allegory, by the very philosophy of the schools she proves his gods are nothing. He cannot answer her and dares not kill her yet. In the place where a philosopher will be unmade, the philosopher-saint stands and speaks — the fold closes tile against tile.
stops.quote: I am Katherine, daughter of Costus the king, and howbeit that I was born in purple, I have despised these things and turned me to the Lord Jesu Christ.
stops.quote_source: Golden Legend (Caxton's translation), Life of Saint Katherine
suggested_refs: Golden Legend, the disputation before the emperor

stops.name: Alexandria — the fifty philosophers converted and burned
stops.campa: The emperor gathers fifty orators and philosophers, the masters of Egypt, to break one girl in argument. She converts them instead: hearing her expound the Incarnation out of their own Sibyls and Plato, the fifty confess Christ together. Maxentius burns them in the midst of the city, and the fire — the canon is exact — consumes neither hair nor garment; the bodies lie whole as sleepers. Fifty philosophers led to God by a virgin of Alexandria: the school of Hypatia, says the fold, refounded in heaven.
suggested_refs: Pinturicchio, 'Disputation of Saint Catherine' (Borgia Apartments)
sources: Golden Legend (Caxton), Life of Saint Katherine

stops.name: Alexandria — the prison: the dove and the empress
stops.campa: Twelve days she lies in a darkened cell without food, and a dove of heaven feeds her, and Christ visits her with light. The empress Faustina comes secretly by night with Porphyrius the captain and two hundred knights to see the prisoner; they find the cell shining and angels anointing her wounds, and all are converted on the spot. The emperor will kill his own wife and his own general before he touches the girl — the story insists on it: her prison converts the palace faster than his palace can empty her prison.
suggested_refs: Golden Legend, the prison visitation
cycle of Saint Catherine frescoes, San Clemente (Masolino)
sources: Golden Legend (Caxton), Life of Saint Katherine

stops.name: Alexandria — the wheel that shatters
stops.campa: The provost Cursates builds the engine: four wheels bound with iron saws and sharp nails, two turning against two, that the virgin may be torn apart as a terror to the city. Katherine prays. An angel of the Lord strikes the machine, and the wheel bursts asunder at her touch with such violence that four thousand of the heathen are slain by its flying wreckage. The instrument becomes her signature: forever after she is known by the broken wheel — the sign that the engines of the world do not survive contact with wisdom.
suggested_refs: the Catherine wheel in iconography and rose windows
Golden Legend, the breaking of the wheels
sources: Golden Legend (Caxton), Life of Saint Katherine

stops.name: Alexandria — the beheading: milk, not blood
stops.campa: Led out to the place of execution, she prays that whoever remembers her passion may be heard, and a voice answers from heaven: Come, my love, my spouse; the door of heaven is opened to thee. The sword falls, and from her body issues milk instead of blood — the sign the canon sets against the tiles of the Caesareum: where the philosopher was opened with shells and gave blood, the saint is opened with steel and gives milk, the drink of teachers, the first food of the soul. Alexandria has killed its wise virgin twice; this time the body will not stay for the fire.
suggested_refs: Golden Legend: 'there issued out of her body milk instead of blood'
Menologion of Basil II, martyrdom of Catherine
sources: Golden Legend (Caxton), Life of Saint Katherine

stops.name: Mount Sinai — Jebel Katherina: the angels lay down the body
stops.campa: Angels take up the body from the killing ground of Alexandria and bear it through the air more than twenty days' journey, to the highest mountain of Sinai — the peak beside the mountain of the Law — and bury it there with honor. The geometry is deliberate: from the city of the murdered philosopher to the mountain where God spoke definitions out of fire. What Cinaron's flames were denied, Sinai's granite receives. The mountain takes her name; from her bones, continually, runs an oil that heals all sickness.
suggested_refs: icons of the Translation of Saint Catherine by angels (Sinai school)
Jebel Katherina, the chapel on the summit
sources: Golden Legend (Caxton), Life of Saint Katherine

stops.name: Mount Sinai — Justinian's fortress-monastery at the Burning Bush
stops.campa: The emperor Justinian walls in the Burning Bush at the mountain's foot — a fortress-church garrisoned with monks, the oldest continuously inhabited monastery in Christendom, its library second only to Rome's. Prophets' ground: here the bush burned and was not consumed, as the fifty philosophers burned and were not consumed. The house does not yet know it is hers; it keeps the Bush and the relics of the Law and waits. Above it, on the higher peak, the buried virgin keeps her own vigil in the granite.
suggested_refs: Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai
Procopius, Buildings V.8
the Christ Pantocrator icon of Sinai

stops.name: Mount Sinai — the invention of the relics: the oil
stops.campa: Guided by a vision, the monks climb the great peak and find her: the body of the virgin of Alexandria, incorrupt in the rock, five centuries dead, the holy oil — the myron — welling from her bones. They carry her down to the fortress of the Bush and lay her in a marble chest beside the sanctuary, and the monastery of the Transfiguration becomes, in the mouths of all pilgrims, Saint Catherine's. The head and the left hand keep the church; the oil goes out in phials to the whole world, and with it her name.
suggested_refs: the marble reliquary sarcophagus of Saint Catherine at Sinai
the 13th-century Sinai icon of Catherine with scenes of her life

stops.name: Mount Sinai — the monk Symeon sets out with the finger
stops.campa: Symeon, monk of Sinai — Sicilian-born, Greek-tongued, guide of pilgrims — is sent west to collect the monastery's alms from the duke of Normandy. As he goes, the legend says, a phalanx detaches itself from one of the virgin's fingers into his keeping: the saint chooses her own courier. He survives Saracen pirates on the Nile and robbers in the passes; the relic rides in his scrip across the whole breadth of the world, from the mountain of the Law toward the rains of Normandy.
suggested_refs: Eberwin of Trier, Vita of Saint Symeon
the pilgrim roads from Sinai to Rouen

stops.name: Rouen — the hill above the city: Sainte-Catherine-du-Mont
stops.campa: On the hill commanding Rouen, Goscelin the viscount founds the abbey of Holy Trinity, and into its altar goes the finger of the virgin of Alexandria and Sinai. The relic swallows the dedication: the abbey becomes Sainte-Catherine-du-Mont and the hill itself the Côte Sainte-Catherine, and Normandy takes her feast — the twenty-fifth of November — into its bones. Miracles gather; pilgrims climb; her legend is preached in Norman French. The philosopher of Alexandria now has a hill over the very city where, four centuries on, a girl who heard her voice will burn.
suggested_refs: the Côte Sainte-Catherine above Rouen
charters of La Trinité-du-Mont / Sainte-Catherine-du-Mont

stops.name: Trier — the Porta Nigra: the courier walled in
stops.campa: His errand done, Symeon of Sinai asks to be buried alive in the east tower of the Porta Nigra, the black Roman gate of Trier, and lives there a recluse until his death on the first day of June, 1035. Within the year, Pope Benedict inscribes him among the saints — among the first men ever canonized by papal decree. So the carrier of Catherine's finger becomes a saint by carrying her: the relay is blessed link by link, and the gate of a dead empire becomes a shrine on the road her cult travels.
suggested_refs: the Porta Nigra and Simeonstift, Trier
Eberwin's Vita Symeonis

stops.name: Domrémy — the garden: Catherine speaks to Joan
stops.campa: In her father's garden at Domrémy, at midday in summer, a peasant girl of thirteen hears a voice from the right, from toward the church, in a great light. Saint Michael comes first; then, as he promised, come Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret, crowned with fair crowns, rich and precious, speaking sweetly and low in the French tongue. The virgin of Alexandria, who out-argued fifty philosophers, takes a pupil who cannot read: for four years she counsels Joan, governs her, and prepares her for the king, the siege, and the sword.
stops.quote: When I was thirteen years old, I had a voice from God to help me govern myself.
stops.quote_source: Joan of Arc, trial testimony, Rouen, 22 February 1431
suggested_refs: the trial record of Joan of Arc (procès de condamnation, BnF)
the basilica of Bois-Chenu at Domrémy
sources: Trial of Condemnation of Joan of Arc (1431), session of 22 February

stops.name: Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois — the chapel in the woods: a sword laid down
stops.campa: In the iron woods of Touraine stands a chapel of Saint Catherine, and the tradition of the place reaches back to Charles Martel: returning from breaking the Saracens between Tours and Poitiers, the Hammer lays his sword behind the altar as an ex-voto to the virgin of the wheel. Centuries of soldiers follow his example; freed prisoners hang their chains on her walls. Under the altar-stone, in the earth, one blade with five crosses settles into its rust and begins to wait. It knows how long. Seven hundred years.
suggested_refs: the church of Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois
the Charles Martel sword tradition

stops.name: Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois — Joan halts at the shrine
stops.campa: Eleven days out of Vaucouleurs, through enemy country in a man's clothes, Joan the Maid comes to rest at the one shrine on her road that bears her counselor's name. At Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois she hears three Masses in a day and dictates her first letter to the Dauphin at Chinon, six leagues on: she has ridden a hundred and fifty leagues to come to his aid, and she knows many things good for him. She sleeps under Catherine's roof, above the buried sword, and says nothing of it yet. Her voices keep their own calendar.
suggested_refs: Joan's dictated letter from Fierbois to the Dauphin (attested at the trial, 27 February 1431)
sources: Trial of Condemnation, session of 27 February 1431

stops.name: Tours — the armorer is sent
stops.campa: At Tours, armed and examined and believed, the Maid refuses the offer of a new sword. Her voices have told her where hers lies: in the church of Saint Catherine at Fierbois, behind the altar, in the ground. She sends an armorer of Tours with a letter to the priests of Fierbois asking that the sword be sought and sent. She has never seen the man who buried it nor the earth that holds it. The clergy of Fierbois take up the pavement behind their altar because a peasant girl wrote to them that a sword was there.
stops.quote: Whilst I was at Tours or at Chinon, I sent to seek for a sword which was in the church of Saint Catherine de Fierbois, behind the altar; it was found there at once; the sword was in the ground, and rusty; upon it were five crosses; I knew it by my voices.
stops.quote_source: Joan of Arc, trial testimony, Rouen, 27 February 1431
suggested_refs: the trial record, session of 27 February 1431
sources: Trial of Condemnation of Joan of Arc, 27 February 1431

stops.name: Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois — the sword found: the circle closes
stops.campa: The priests dig behind the altar and the earth gives up the blade: rusted through, five crosses on the steel. They rub it, and the rust falls away at once, without effort — a thousand years of waiting shed like a husk. The clergy of Fierbois sheath it in red velvet; Joan will carry it to Orléans and Patay and never, she swears, kill a man with it. Here the journey ends and hands itself on: the wisdom of Alexandria, burned at Cinaron, crowned at Sinai, carried to Normandy, has put its sword into the hand of the girl. Catherine's road ends where Joan's begins.
stops.quote: After this sword was found, the prelates of the place had it rubbed, and at once the rust fell from it without difficulty.
stops.quote_source: Joan of Arc, trial testimony, Rouen, 27 February 1431
suggested_refs: the sword of Fierbois with five crosses (lost; described in the trial record)
the church of Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois, rebuilt in her honor
sources: Trial of Condemnation of Joan of Arc, 27 February 1431
